## If You Cannot Test It, You Cannot Claim It Works

Theory is beautiful. Simulations are convincing. But a control law that works perfectly in a linearized model can catastrophically fail on hardware if one number is wrong. The only honest way forward is to *measure* every claim: Does the linearization actually approximate the nonlinear flow? Is the contraction margin really there, or did numerical error eat it? Do real trajectories actually stay within the predicted envelope under worst-case disturbances? This chapter is a checklist for answering these questions.

## Introduction and Qualitative Purpose

This chapter defines reproducibility and validation standards required for a textbook-quality treatment.

## In Laymans Terms

Every equation should be testable, and every claim should have a measurable check.

## Geometric Intuition

For each derivation, identify the perturbation object, metric object, and decay/optimality claim being made.

## Minimum Validation Checklist

1. Finite-difference check for all linearizations.
2. Conditioning audit for Riccati factors and metric matrices.
3. Residual spectrum logs for contraction inequalities.
4. Monte Carlo perturbation rollouts against predicted decay.
5. Sensitivity sweeps under parameter and contact-model mismatch.
